transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-14
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ravi (Redwood SE), Jenna (Velcrum CTO), Omar (Velcrum Sr. Platform Eng), Lea (Velcrum Data Scientist)

Optional auto-generated sections:
Summary: (auto) Customer wants low-latency search assistant, concerns about PII, wants on-prem or VPC eval, will likely pilot Dedicated if costs align.
Topics: hosted/de-dedicated/private, sdk, langchain, proxy, quotas, observability
Action items: see metadata

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Okay, hi everybody, thanks for taking the time. I'm Maya from Redwood Inference, AE on the account. Ravi from solutions engineering is here for the technical bits. Uh, Jenna, Omar, Lea, thanks for joining. Can you give a quick intro on goals?
[00:12] Jenna: Yeah hi, thanks. We're Velcrum Systems. We run an enterprise search product embedded in a couple SaaS apps. We're experimenting with an LLM search assistant that re-ranks results and drafts short summaries. Main constraints are: PII handling, latency under 250ms p90 for short queries, and predictable cost. We're evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[00:30] Ravi: Great. Quick clarifying Q: when you say PII handling, is that data residency, or do you have a redaction pipeline before it goes out?
[00:38] Omar: A bit of both. We have a pre-redact pass but some requests still contain named entities. Ideally we'd like no customer cloud egress for certain tenants — need VPC or private on-prem for regulated clients.
[00:49] Maya: Understood — good candidates for Redwood Private or a Dedicated with VPC peering depending on throughput.
[00:56] Lea: Also: integrations — we use Python backend, and a small Node edge for websockets. We use LangChain for orchestration and LlamaIndex for our document store connectors — how mature are Redwood SDKs with those?
[01:10] Ravi: Our Python and Node SDKs are first-class. We have example LangChain chains and a LlamaIndex connector in the repo — I can point you to the sample notebooks. They support streaming responses, function calling metadata, and chunked embeddings pipelines. The LangChain examples show both sync and async patterns but note: sometimes small api surface naming differs, e.g., 'client.generate' vs 'llm.generate' — it's mostly ergonomic though.
[01:34] Jenna: Cool. For the LangChain integration, how does Redwood handle tokenization/contexts — specifically if we rely on long-context retrieval, does Redwood support KV cache reuse across calls to lower tokens?
[01:45] Ravi: Yes — the runtime maintains key-value cache where compatible. For hosted we expose automatic KV prefix caching for repeated prompts; on Dedicated/Private you can configure cache persistence windows, and there's options for pinned KV shards in dedicated GPU pools to keep latency low. Small caveat: cross-shard cache reuse depends on your routing — if we route between different model variants we may not reuse all keys.
[02:09] Omar: That routing bit — can we pin traffic so single-tenant queries always land on the same model pool? We want consistent latency for SLAs.
[02:17] Maya: For Dedicated you can reserve capacity and pin model versions and routing policies to keep traffic local. For hosted you'd rely on routing policies and can request affinity but it's less strict. Private gives you full control if you deploy within your VPC or on-prem.
[02:29] Lea: On the gateway/proxy front: our infra team prefers to put a light-weight gateway in front of external APIs for audit and rate limiting. Does Redwood recommend a proxy pattern or using the SDK directly from the backend?
[02:41] Ravi: Both are valid. A common pattern: edge proxy that handles multi-tenant auth and per-tenant quotas, then server-side services call Redwood SDK with service credentials. That way you centralize rate-limits and logging in your gateway. We also offer an ingest-side tokenization helper if you want to offload heavy pre-processing.
[03:00] Jenna: How do rate-limits and quotas map? We need per-tenant soft limits and hard limits e.g., 5 req/s per tenant, and a global account cap. Also alerting when tenants hit 80% usage.
[03:10] Ravi: Redwood supports per-token and per-route quotas, and you can configure per-customer rate policies in Dedicated and Private. Hosted has per-api-key quotas and also per-route throttling. We expose webhooks for quota events and metric streams to your observability stack.
[03:26] Omar: What observability hooks are available? We want per-request traces, token-level timing, and end-to-end latencies to correlate with our logs.
[03:34] Ravi: We have tracing hooks compatible with OpenTelemetry, per-request metadata (model, sequence_len, cost_tokens), and granular cost breakdowns. You can ingest these into your APM, or we can stream into a customer-owned S3 for longer retention. There are also per-model dashboards in Redwood Console with tail-latency histograms and token burn reports.
[03:55] Lea: Any sample dashboards or Grafana panels?
[03:58] Ravi: Yes, we'll share a dashboard JSON and sample Kibana/Grafana queries.
[04:03] Jenna: Security controls — SSO, SAML, RBAC, and KMS/HSM for keys — what does Redwood support?
[04:11] Maya: We support SAML SSO for Console, RBAC with fine-grained roles, and in Private/Dedicated you can bring your own KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or HSM) for encryption at rest and for customer-managed key rotation. Hosted supports envelope encryption and keys managed in Redwood but we can discuss a dedicated key path if needed for enterprise plans.
[04:34] Omar: For audit logs — we need immutable logs for model inputs and outputs for the regulated tenants, retention 7 years, and export to our SIEM. Is that realistic?
[04:44] Ravi: We provide audit logs with configurable retention; for hosted longer retention is an add-on. For Private you manage storage, so 7 years is feasible. Note you must consider privacy/regulatory constraints if logs contain PII — we can redact or hash sensitive fields before persisting.
[05:01] Jenna: Good point. For model variants — we may want a smaller quantized model for baseline and fallback to larger model when quality matters. Can Redwood orchestrate multi-model fallbacks?
[05:12] Ravi: Yes, routing policies allow you to define fallbacks by latency/cost/quality. For example, route to quantized 4-bit variant for most requests and fallback to a higher-precision variant if confidence metrics are low or if user requests a 'high-quality' option. We expose automatic A/B rollouts and can do canary percentages per-model.
[05:34] Lea: About latency budgets — you mentioned p90 250ms as target. How realistic is that on Dedicated vs Hosted for a 1k token prompt?
[05:44] Ravi: For short prompts (under 256 tokens) Dedicated with optimized kernels + pinned KV can get well under 250ms p90 on modern GPUs. For 1k tokens it's more variable — shared hosted pools may see higher tail latency unless you configure higher tier capacity. Quantization helps, but sequence length dominates compute. We'll validate with a benchmark.
[06:05] Omar: Benchmarks — what tooling do you suggest? We need to replicate our traffic patterns: mix of short re-rank, medium summarization, and long doc extraction (1k+).
[06:15] Ravi: We'll provide a benchmarking script that supports a mixed workload, traces token timings, and emits OpenTelemetry spans. We'll run it on Dedicated pilot pool and provide results. Need your sample queries and a small corpus to seed the KV cache behavior.
[06:28] Jenna: Sounds good. Cost — how do you recommend we estimate cost per-tenant? We need to model worst-case and steady-state.
[06:36] Maya: We provide per-token pricing and Dedicated capacity pricing. For Dedicated we can estimate amortized cost per request using utilization rates; Redwood Optimize can suggest batching and cache settings to lower cost. We'll put together a few scenarios in the pricing doc.
[06:50] Omar: On the integration side, any gotchas when using LangChain or LlamaIndex with streaming responses and function-calling? We rely on function calling for structured outputs.
[06:59] Ravi: Streaming + function-calling is supported. The main caveat is ensuring your chain handles partial streams gracefully — our SDK provides helper callbacks to buffer and then call your function handler once the full structure is available, but we've seen some customers need a small adapter layer because LangChain's event model and SDK event model differ slightly. We'll share a small adapter snippet.
[07:18] Lea: Do you have sample code for the Node websocket edge + Python backend pattern?
[07:23] Ravi: Yes, example repo includes an edge proxy pattern using express/ws for Node and a Python service with the SDK. We'll link those.
[07:29] Jenna: On the private/on-prem option — what's the deployment footprint? We have 8 GPU nodes in our colo, can Redwood runtime run in our cluster?
[07:39] Maya: Yes, Redwood Private includes a runtime you can deploy in your k8s cluster or on dedicated machines. We'll need to check kernel compatibility and driver versions. For on-prem we ship a private control plane connector; metrics stay in your network. There's also a hybrid mode where the control plane is hosted but inference nodes are in your VPC.
[07:58] Omar: Network egress — if we do Private with a hosted control plane, what metadata is sent to Redwood?
[08:04] Ravi: Metadata required for control plane: non-sensitive telemetry and health signals. You can opt out of some telemetry. No customer-payloads are stored in hosted control plane unless you enable telemetry exports — for regulated tenants you'd choose on-prem control plane. We'll provide the exact data flow docs.
[08:20] Jenna: Any references of customers in our space that use Dedicated or Private?
[08:24] Maya: We can share anonymized case studies — e.g., an enterprise in FinTech that moved regulated workloads to Private with KMS and saw tail-latency improvement after pinning KV. I'll include that in follow up.
[08:34] Omar: PCI/PII compliance — do you do SOC 2 Type II? What's the audit scope?
[08:39] Maya: Yes, Redwood is SOC 2 Type II; we also have ISO 27001 summary for certain releases. We'll attach the certs in the security pack.
[08:49] Lea: One more on quotas — if a tenant exceeds quota, can we set graceful degradation behavior? E.g., fall back to cached responses or a smaller model?
[08:58] Ravi: Absolutely. You can configure automatic fallbacks: serve stale cached answer, downgrade to a cheaper quantized model, or reject with a soft error. These can be enforced at your gateway or at Redwood routing policies.
[09:12] Jenna: Great. Operational runbook — we'd want steps for incident: high tail latency, model regression detection, or cost spike. Do you have templated runbooks?
[09:20] Maya: Yes, Redwood Console includes alerts we recommend and we share runbook templates for common incidents, plus a playbook for automatic rollback to previous model version.
[09:30] Omar: Any limitations on model licensing or allowed model families for Private? We sometimes need to bring Llama 3 variants.
[09:38] Ravi: You can bring your own model artifacts for Private if licensing permits. For hosted we curate models and provide Redwood-verified variants. We'll walk through onboarding steps and packaging requirements for BYO models.
[09:50] Lea: OK, sounds like a path forward. Can we agree on pilot scope? Maybe Dedicated pilot for 2 weeks with mixed workload, 3 tenants including one regulated tenant on a private VPC peering?
[09:59] Maya: That seems reasonable. Action items: we'll provision a small Dedicated pool, share benchmark script, and send security docs.
[10:07] Jenna: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[10:10] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up with links and set next meeting for results review.

End of transcript.
